     24	---
     25	# Amazon EBS Expertise
     26	
     27	Use this skill to troubleshoot Amazon EBS problems and to review an account's Amazon EBS setup. It has two modes. Troubleshoot mode answers "something is wrong, why?" through one of five paths and returns a fixed verdict. Review mode answers "is my EBS setup healthy before something goes wrong?" and returns a rated report. Both modes are read-only and share the same volume-type rules, instance limits and service rules. Load only the reference files the request needs.
     28	
     29	## When to Use This Skill
     30	
     31	- Storage-related slowness, timeouts or high I/O latency on an Amazon EC2 instance.
     32	- An alarm on AWS/EBS metrics or on instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%`.
     33	- A request to raise IOPS or throughput, or to modify a volume.
     34	- A volume modification that looks stuck, failed, or did not improve performance.
     35	- Snapshot, AMI, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, AWS Backup or Recycle Bin questions, including which snapshots need owner review before deletion.
     36	- Encrypted-volume access errors and AWS KMS questions for Amazon EBS.
     37	- Amazon EBS cost increases, idle or over-provisioned volumes.
     38	- An operation that failed on an Amazon EBS quota, or "how close am I to my limits?"
     39	- A request to review Amazon EBS posture before a launch, migration or peak event.
     40	
     41	Do not use this skill for Amazon S3, Amazon EFS, Amazon FSx, instance store, or Amazon EC2 issues unrelated to Amazon EBS.
     42	
     43	## Prerequisites
     44	
     45	- Read-only permissions for the APIs listed in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md).
     46	- AWS CloudTrail access is optional. The skill works without it.
     47	- Mutating changes run only through directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App), which need their own role and operator approval on the approval card.
     48	
     49	---
     50	
     51	## Workflow
     52	
     53	Copy this checklist and tick each step as you finish it:
     54	
     55	- [ ] Step 1: Classify the request
     56	- [ ] Step 2: Load the shared references
     57	- [ ] Step 3: Run the path and draft the report
     58	- [ ] Step 4: Check the draft, fix it, then present it
     59	
     60	## Step 1: Classify the Request
     61	
     62	| The user says or the alarm shows | Mode and path | Load |
     63	|---|---|---|
     64	| "My app is slow", high latency, an alarm on AWS/EBS metrics, `EBSIOBalance%` or `EBSByteBalance%`, "is it storage?", "how much IOPS do I need?" | Troubleshoot: performance | [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md) |
     65	| "My modification is stuck", "the new IOPS has not taken effect", a `ModifyVolume` error, resize, gp2 to gp3, extend the file system, shrink or cancel | Troubleshoot: volume modification | [references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md](references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md) |
     66	| "Which snapshots can I delete?", snapshot copy did not arrive, AMI creation stuck, recover a deleted snapshot or volume, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, Recycle Bin | Troubleshoot: snapshots | [references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md](references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md) |
     67	| "I can't attach my KMS-encrypted volume", share an encrypted snapshot or AMI, encryption by default, re-encrypt a volume | Troubleshoot: encryption | [references/troubleshoot-encryption.md](references/troubleshoot-encryption.md) |
     68	| "Why did my EBS bill go up?", unexplained charges, idle or unattached volumes, pricing model | Troubleshoot: billing | [references/troubleshoot-billing.md](references/troubleshoot-billing.md) |
     69	| "Limit exceeded", a quota error, "how close am I to my limits?" | Shared capability: quota headroom | [Capacity and quota headroom](references/review-operational.md#capacity-and-quota-headroom) |
     70	| "Are my volumes backed up?" | Review: resilience area | [Resilience](references/review-operational.md#resilience) |
     71	| "Review my EBS setup", "is my storage production-ready?" | Review | [references/review-operational.md](references/review-operational.md) and [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md) |
     72	
     73	If a request fits more than one row, answer the question the user asked first and treat the rest as Separate findings.
     74	
     75	## Step 2: Load the Shared References
     76	
     77	- Always load [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md) (read-only APIs, metric math, errors and fallbacks).
     78	- Load [references/metrics-thresholds.md](references/metrics-thresholds.md) for any metric judgement.
     79	- Load [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md) for the verdict, the binding layer, escalation and review ratings.
     80	- Load [references/ebs-best-practices.md](references/ebs-best-practices.md) for service rules (Elastic Volumes, instance limits, quotas, snapshots, quirks).
     81	
     82	## Step 3: Run the Path and Draft the Report
     83	
     84	Follow the numbered procedure in the loaded path. Discover every value from the APIs. Then draft the report in the format below.
     85	
     86	### Troubleshoot verdict format
     87	
     88	1. **Answer:** the asked question, answered first.
     89	2. **Evidence:** values with units and time window.
     90	3. **Binding layer:** Volume, Instance, Burst credits, Quota, Not EBS, AWS-side impairment (only with a direct signal, see [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md)), Indeterminate, or Not applicable.
     91	4. **Recommendation:** exact parameters, or "No change".
     92	5. **Separate findings:** other true facts that do not change the Answer.
     93	6. **Gaps:** what could not be checked and why.
     94	
     95	In an investigation, put the Answer and the Recommendation with its exact parameters in the root cause finding, not only under Gaps. Keep the findings on the resource the user asked about. Mention another volume only when it shares the same instance EBS baseline, and then as a Separate finding.
     96	
     97	When the Binding layer is Indeterminate, report it as one finding. Do not offer AWS-side impairment as a hypothesis. List each direct check you ran (volume status, `VolumeStalledIOCheck`, AWS Health, AWS FIS) with its result as supporting evidence, say that no check confirms or rules out an EBS-side slowdown, and give the escalation path.
     98	
     99	Review mode uses the rated report in [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md). Every Review mode response MUST begin with its Summary table, which rates all six areas (capacity and quota headroom, observability, cost hygiene, resilience, encryption posture, deletion protection), even when an area has no findings or is `Indeterminate`. The Summary table is required, not optional. Do not open with prose or an offer to run the review; start with the table, then the per-area detail.
     100	
     101	## Step 4: Check the Draft Before Presenting It
     102	
     103	Review the draft from Step 3 against these checks. Fix anything that fails, then present it.
     104	
     105	- Every number under Evidence came from an API call made in this session, has its unit and time window, and matches the resource ID it is attributed to.
     106	- The Binding layer agrees with the Evidence: the named layer is the one at its limit, and the other layers were checked and shown to have headroom. The Evidence gives the instance EBS baseline in MiB/s and IOPS next to the summed demand of all attached volumes.
     107	- Any Recommendation stays within the instance's EBS baseline and the volume type's documented limits, and it is not more provisioning for an impairment.
     108	- Every snapshot tier is backed by the checks it requires; if one of those checks failed, the item is not listed for owner review. No snapshot is recommended for deletion; the owner confirms first.
     109	- A review answer starts with the Summary table and rates all six areas.
     110	- Every API that failed or was not called is listed under Gaps.
     111	
     112	---
     113	
     114	## Critical Rules
     115	
     116	- **Read-only.** Changes (ModifyVolume, quota requests) are proposed with exact parameters, cost and rollback, and run only through operator-approved directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App). Approval is given only on the approval card. A typed "approve" in chat is not approval.
     117	- **Deletes are manual customer steps.** AWS DevOps Agent refuses delete-class operations (for example DeleteSnapshot, DeleteVolume, DeregisterImage), so never propose them as directed actions. After the owner confirms they no longer need the resource, give the commands for the customer to run with their own credentials.
     118	- **Answer in one reply.** In chat, run the checks in this conversation and return the finished verdict or report as your reply. Do not hand the work to a background sub-agent and reply with a "started" or "I will report back" message, because that message becomes the answer the user sees first.
     119	- **Discover, don't assume:** read every configuration value from the APIs.
     120	- **Rule EBS in or out before tuning it.**
     121	- **Answer the asked question first;** other findings go under "Separate findings".
     122	- **Review mode starts with the Summary table.** Every Review mode response begins with the Summary table of all six rated areas. The table is required, not optional.
     123	- **Always check the instance layer** and size changes within the instance's EBS **baseline**.
     124	- **Never recommend more provisioning for an impairment.**
     125	- **Use current service rules:** up to 4 Elastic Volumes modifications per volume per rolling 24 hours. There is no fixed waiting period between modifications; the next one is allowed once the previous one completes.
     126	- **No interpretation without data:** report what couldn't be checked and use fallbacks. `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the most recent modification per volume; modification history and counts come from the optional AWS CloudTrail `ModifyVolume` events, or are listed under Gaps.
     127	- **Units:** MiB/s for throughput, stated every time.
     128	- **Escalate** on scope signals or when the investigation can't explain the symptom.
     129	
     130	## Gotchas
     131	
     132	- A modification in `optimizing` is not stuck. The new size, IOPS or throughput already applies while it optimizes.
     133	- `DescribeInstanceTypes` reports EBS bandwidth in MB/s. Convert it to MiB/s before comparing it with volume throughput.
     134	- On io1 and io2, `VolumeThroughputPercentage` is the percentage of provisioned IOPS delivered. It is not a throughput signal.
     135	- `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `VolumeAvgReadLatency` and `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` need both `VolumeId` and `InstanceId` and exist only on Nitro instances. `VolumeAvgThroughput` is in KiB/s. `VolumeTotalReadTime` and `VolumeTotalWriteTime` are in seconds.
     136	- Rising latency and queue length with falling IOPS is not proof of an AWS-side impairment. Without a direct signal (failed `VolumeStalledIOCheck`, impaired volume status, or an open AWS Health event) and without a running AWS FIS experiment, the Binding layer is Indeterminate.
     137	- `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the latest modification per volume. It cannot count modifications in the last 24 hours.
     138	- `ListRecoveryPointsByResource` without `ManagedByAWSBackupOnly` set to true also lists snapshots that AWS Backup did not create.
     139	- A snapshot whose source volume is gone may be the only remaining copy of the data. List it for owner review; never call it safe to delete.
     140	- Snapshots are incremental, so deleting one may free less storage than its size suggests.
     141	
     142	## Error Handling
     143	
     144	Errors, gated reads and missing metrics are handled with the fallback table in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md). Name every failed API under Gaps and continue with the rest.
     145

{"id": "b6a567b5-8842-44f1-b7eb-a3ffcfceaf4e", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_Em0le7fd0fk4tlYAKdkeSU", "content": [{"text": "     1	# Data collection: read-only APIs, metric math, errors and fallbacks
     2	
     3	Load this file on every request. Every value in a verdict or a review comes from one of these calls. Tags are used for naming only, never as the source of a configuration value.
     4	
     5	## Read-only API allowlist
     6	
     7	| Service | APIs |
     8	|---|---|
     9	| Amazon EC2 | `DescribeVolumes`, `DescribeVolumeStatus`, `DescribeVolumesModifications`, `DescribeVolumeAttribute`, `DescribeInstances`, `DescribeInstanceTypes`, `DescribeInstanceAttribute`, `DescribeSnapshots`, `DescribeSnapshotAttribute`, `DescribeImages`, `DescribeFastSnapshotRestores`, `GetEbsEncryptionByDefault`, `GetEbsDefaultKmsKeyId`, `GetSnapshotBlockPublicAccessState`, `DescribeLockedSnapshots` |
     10	| Amazon CloudWatch | `DescribeAlarms`, `DescribeAlarmHistory`, `GetMetricData`, `ListMetrics` |
     11	| Service Quotas | `ListServiceQuotas`, `GetServiceQuota`, `GetAWSDefaultServiceQuota`, `ListRequestedServiceQuotaChangeHistoryByQuota` |
     12	| Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager | `GetLifecyclePolicies`, `GetLifecyclePolicy` |
     13	| Recycle Bin | `ListRules`, `GetRule` |
     14	| AWS Backup | `ListBackupPlans`, `ListBackupSelections`, `GetBackupSelection`, `ListRecoveryPointsByResource` (always with `ManagedByAWSBackupOnly` set to true; without it the call also returns snapshots AWS Backup did not create), `ListProtectedResources` |
     15	| AWS KMS | `DescribeKey`, `GetKeyPolicy`, `ListGrants` |
     16	| AWS Cost Explorer | `GetCostAndUsage`, `GetDimensionValues` |
     17	| AWS FIS | `ListExperiments`, `GetExperiment` |
     18	| AWS Health | `DescribeEvents` |
     19	| AWS Compute Optimizer (optional) | `GetEBSVolumeRecommendations` |
     20	| AWS CloudTrail (optional) | `LookupEvents`. This call is optional. If it is denied or returns nothing, record a Gap and continue. Never make it a required step |
     21	
     22	Nothing outside this list is called by the skill on its own. Mutating calls are proposals (see SKILL.md Critical rules).
     23	
     24	## Metric rules
     25	
     26	AWS/EBS publishes 1-minute data.
     27	
     28	| Namespace | Metrics | Dimensions |
     29	|---|---|---|
     30	| AWS/EBS | `VolumeAvgIOPS` (Ops/s), `VolumeAvgThroughput` (KiB/s), `VolumeAvgReadLatency` (milliseconds), `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` (milliseconds), `VolumeStalledIOCheck` (0 passed, 1 failed) | `VolumeId` AND `InstanceId`. Nitro instances only |
     31	| AWS/EBS | `VolumeReadOps`, `VolumeWriteOps`, `VolumeReadBytes`, `VolumeWriteBytes`, `VolumeTotalReadTime` (seconds), `VolumeTotalWriteTime` (seconds), `VolumeQueueLength`, `VolumeIdleTime` (seconds), `BurstBalance`, `VolumeThroughputPercentage` (Provisioned IOPS SSD only) | `VolumeId` |
     32	| AWS/EC2 | `EBSIOBalance%`, `EBSByteBalance%`, `EBSReadOps`, `EBSWriteOps`, `EBSReadBytes`, `EBSWriteBytes` | `InstanceId` |
     33	
     34	Metric math from the Amazon CloudWatch metrics page for Amazon EBS. Use `Sum` statistics for ops, bytes and time.
     35	
     36	- IOPS = Sum(`VolumeReadOps` + `VolumeWriteOps`) / period in seconds
     37	- MiB/s = Sum(`VolumeReadBytes` + `VolumeWriteBytes`) / period in seconds / 1,048,576
     38	- Average read latency in milliseconds per operation = Sum(`VolumeTotalReadTime`, in seconds) / Sum(`VolumeReadOps`) x 1,000 (and the write equivalent with `VolumeTotalWriteTime` and `VolumeWriteOps`). Without the x 1,000 the result is in seconds. Always state latency in milliseconds
     39	- Idle percentage = Sum(`VolumeIdleTime`) / period in seconds x 100
     40	- MiB/s from `VolumeAvgThroughput` = value in KiB/s / 1,024
     41	
     42	What a 1-minute average hides: sub-minute peaks can reach a limit while the minute average looks below it (micro-bursting). When latency or queue length rises while the average sits below the limit, say that headroom is not proven instead of claiming it.
     43	
     44	`EBSIOBalance%` and `EBSByteBalance%` are published only for some instance sizes (generally 4xlarge and smaller) that can burst. If they are absent, the instance does not publish them. That is not a fault.
     45	
     46	## Errors and fallbacks
     47	
     48	| What happens | What it means | What to do |
     49	|---|---|---|
     50	| `AccessDenied` on any call | The role cannot read that data | Name the exact API in Gaps. Continue with the rest |
     51	| A read call is held behind an operator-approval gate (for example `dlm:GetLifecyclePolicies` or `rbin:ListRules`) | The Agent Space treats it as an action | Report it as a Gap and say which conclusion stays unconfirmed. Never ask the operator to bypass the gate |
     52	| No `VolumeAvg*` data | The instance is not Nitro, or the `InstanceId` dimension is missing | Add `InstanceId`. If still empty, use the Sum-based math above |
     53	| `EBSIOBalance%` absent | The instance size does not publish it | Compare the summed IOPS and MiB/s of all attached volumes to the `DescribeInstanceTypes` baseline |
     54	| `DescribeInstanceTypes` values in MB/s | The API reports instance throughput in MB/s (bandwidth in Mbps) | Convert to MiB/s before comparing (1 MB/s = 1,000,000 bytes/s; 1 MiB/s = 1,048,576 bytes/s) |
     55	| AWS CloudTrail optional lookup denied or empty | No access, or the event is older than the 90 days that `LookupEvents` covers | Use `DescribeVolumesModifications` for the current or latest modification only; it returns only the most recent modification per volume. Record a Gap for the modification history and for the 24-hour modification count |
     56	| No metric data for a volume | The volume is new, detached, or the window is wrong | Check `DescribeVolumes` state and attachment times, widen the window, report the Gap |
     57	
     58	## Sources
     59	
     60	- Amazon CloudWatch metrics for Amazon EBS (units, dimensions, `VolumeStalledIOCheck` with `VolumeId` and `InstanceId`, and the latency formula Sum(`VolumeTotalReadTime`) / Sum(`VolumeReadOps`) x 1000 in ms/op): https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/using_cloudwatch_ebs.html
     61	- Instance metrics, including `EBSIOBalance%` and `EBSByteBalance%`: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/viewing_metrics_with_cloudwatch.html
     62	- Amazon EBS-optimized instances (baseline and maximum, MB/s): https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/ebs-optimized.html
     63	- Monitoring volume modifications: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/monitoring-volume-modifications.html
     64	- DescribeVolumesModifications (most recent modification request only): https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/APIReference/API_DescribeVolumesModifications.html
     65	- AWS CloudTrail LookupEvents (last 90 days): https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/APIReference/API_LookupEvents.html
     66	- AWS FIS actions: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/fis/latest/userguide/fis-actions-reference.html"}], "status": "success", "type": "tool_result"}, {"id": "tooluse_CnKeKpJmbsOx6BI701UjX0", "content": [{"text": "     1	# Finding logic: verdict template, binding layer, escalation, review ratings
     2	
     3	## Troubleshoot verdict template
     4	
     5	Every troubleshoot answer uses these six headings in this order.
     6	
     7	1. **Answer.** The question the user asked, answered first in one or two sentences. For example "Not stuck. The modification is in `optimizing`, which already applies the new IOPS."
     8	2. **Evidence.** The values that support the answer, each with units and the time window (for example "average `<value>` IOPS, `<start>` to `<end>` UTC"). Throughput in MiB/s.

     14	## Binding-layer decision tree
     15	
     16	Work through it in order. Use measured values and the limits read from the APIs. Do not use fixed percentage triggers.
     17

     22	3. Is a gp2, st1 or sc1 volume's `BurstBalance` draining or at 0?

     5	## Elastic Volumes rules
     6	
     7	- You can make up to 4 modifications to a volume in a rolling 24-hour period. There is no fixed waiting period between modifications; the next one is allowed once the previous one completes (January 2026 change).
     8	- Size can only increase. It cannot be reduced. To get a smaller volume, create a new volume and copy the data.
     9	- A modification request cannot be cancelled after it is submitted.
     10	- States are `modifying`, then `optimizing`, then `completed` (or `failed`). In `optimizing` the new configuration already applies, and performance is between the source and the target. The modification completes on its own.
     11	- Duration is best effort. The Amazon EBS User Guide says a 1 TiB volume typically takes up to about six hours to modify, and some performance changes take more than 24 hours, for example when the volume is not fully initialized.
     12	- After a size increase, the operating system must extend the partition and the file system. The agent gives the commands; the operator runs them.
     13	- Read the requirements page before proposing a change on an older instance, or on a volume with an MBR partition (2 TiB limit).

     15	## Instance EBS layer
     16	
     17	- All volumes attached to an instance share the instance's EBS bandwidth, IOPS and throughput. Sum the measured values across all attached volumes, including the root volume.
     18	- Size any target within the instance's EBS baseline from `DescribeInstanceTypes`, not its burst maximum.

     48	- gp3: IOPS and throughput are provisioned independently. Compare actual IOPS to Iops AND actual MiB/s to Throughput; either can bind.
     49	- gp2: baseline IOPS = 3 x GiB (min 100), burst to 3,000 while BurstBalance > 0. Check BurstBalance draining or at 0.
     50	- io1/io2 (incl. Block Express): compare actual IOPS to provisioned Iops AND actual MiB/s to the volume's throughput limit; either can bind. Throughput is not provisioned separately, but the documented throughput limit depends on the provisioned IOPS (see the io1 and io2 rows in [metrics-thresholds.md](metrics-thresholds.md)). Compute the limit from `Iops` with those rules, then compare. Do NOT use VolumeThroughputPercentage to judge throughput on io1/io2; it reports the % of provisioned IOPS delivered.
     51	- st1/sc1: throughput-oriented with burst credits; compare MiB/s to the baseline/burst for the size and check BurstBalance.
     52	- Judge io1, io2 and gp3 by both IOPS and throughput. Per-type limits are in [metrics-thresholds.md](metrics-thresholds.md).
     53	
     54	### Step 4: Check the instance layer
     55	
     56	- Sum actual IOPS and MiB/s across all attached volumes; compare to the instance type's EBS baseline from DescribeInstanceTypes.
     57	- Aggregate across ALL attached volumes, including the root volume.
     58	- Check EBSIOBalance% / EBSByteBalance%. If they are draining or at 0, or the sum is at the instance limit, the INSTANCE is the binding layer and raising volume provisioning will not help.
     59	- If instance metrics are healthy and a volume is at its own limit, the VOLUME is the binding layer.
     60	- If `EBSIOBalance%` is absent, the instance size does not publish it. Use the summed values against the baseline.
     61	
     62	### Step 5: Distinguish saturation from impairment
     63	
     64	If queue length and latency are elevated but the volume and instance are both below their limits, this is NOT saturation. Suspect an impairment or injected latency; do NOT recommend increasing provisioning.
     65	
     66	The impairment signature is IOPS and throughput collapsing while latency and `VolumeQueueLength` rise. Saturation looks different: metrics flat at the provisioned limit with modest latency. When you see the impairment signature, check in this order:
     67	
     68	1. The `DescribeVolumeStatus` result from Step 2 (impaired status, failing checks, scheduled events). Read it again if the symptom started after Step 2.
     69	2. The `VolumeStalledIOCheck` metric for the volume (dimensions `VolumeId` AND `InstanceId`, Nitro instances only; 0 passed, 1 failed). A failed check (value 1) means the volume's IO is stalled, which is an AWS-side impairment. Escalate per the rules in [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md) and never recommend adding IOPS.
     70	3. AWS Health `DescribeEvents` for Amazon EBS and Amazon EC2 events in the Region and Availability Zone.
     71	4. AWS FIS `ListExperiments` for a running experiment that targets the volume or instance, with actions `aws:ebs:volume-io-latency` or `aws:ebs:pause-volume-io`. If one is running, say so plainly: the latency is injected and will end with the experiment.
     72	
     73	Name AWS-side impairment only when item 1, 2 or 3 gives a direct signal (an impaired status or failed status check, a failed `VolumeStalledIOCheck`, or an open AWS Health event). If none of the four explains it, report the Binding layer as Indeterminate, keep the cause open, tell the customer to check the AWS Health Dashboard and the volume status checks, and follow the escalation rules in [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md).
     74	
     75	### Step 5b: Recent changes (optional)
     76	
     77	Read `DescribeVolumesModifications` for every attached volume first. It returns only the most recent modification of each volume, so it shows the latest change and its state, not the full history. For earlier changes, an AWS CloudTrail `LookupEvents` search for `ModifyVolume`, `AttachVolume`, `DetachVolume` and `ModifyInstanceAttribute` is optional and only if available. If it is denied or empty, note under Gaps that only the latest modification per volume was checked, and continue.
     78	
     79	### Step 6: Report
     80	
     81	For each affected volume: type, provisioned vs actual, the binding dimension, and whether the volume or the instance is the binding layer. Recommend specific Elastic Volumes changes with target values (raise IOPS, raise gp3 throughput, change type, e.g. gp2 -> gp3), or an instance type change if the instance is the limit. Use MiB/s for throughput.
     82	
     83	Write the report with the verdict template in [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md) (Answer, Evidence, Binding layer, Recommendation, Separate findings, Gaps).
     84	
     85	Elastic Volumes rules: up to 4 modifications per volume in a rolling 24-hour window; each must finish (modifying -> optimizing -> completed) before the next can start. There is no fixed waiting period between modifications; the next one is allowed once the previous one completes (January 2026 change). Rollback is possible once the modification completes, within that limit.
     86	
     87	Sizing rules for any recommended target:
     88	
     89	- Keep the SUM of all volumes attached to the instance within the instance's EBS BASELINE (DescribeInstanceTypes), not its burst maximum. If the target would exceed it, say so and lower the target, or recommend an instance type change.
     90	- gp3 throughput must not exceed 0.25 MiB/s per provisioned IOPS.
     91	- For io1 and io2, the throughput the volume can deliver depends on the provisioned IOPS. If measured MiB/s is at the throughput limit for the current IOPS, a higher IOPS value raises that limit, up to the documented maximum for the type (see [metrics-thresholds.md](metrics-thresholds.md)).
     92	- State how the target was computed (measured demand, type rule, instance baseline minus other volumes' usage).
     93	
     94	## Other performance topics
     95	
     96	### Micro-bursting
     97	
     98	AWS/EBS data is 1-minute. Sub-minute peaks can reach a limit while the minute average stays below it. If latency or queue length rises while the average is below the limit, say that micro-bursting is possible and that headroom is not proven. Do not claim headroom from the average alone.
     99	
     100	### Volume initialization after restore
     101	
     102	A volume created from a snapshot loads blocks from Amazon S3 the first time they are read, which adds latency until the volume is initialized. Check `DescribeVolumes` `SnapshotId` and `CreateTime`. If the volume was recently restored, explain initialization and point to fast snapshot restore (`DescribeFastSnapshotRestores`) and the initialization guide. This is not a provisioning problem.
     103	
     104	### Burst credits
     105	
     106	- Volume level: gp2, st1 and sc1 publish `BurstBalance`. Draining or at 0 means the volume has dropped or will drop to its baseline. Recommend gp2 to gp3 migration, or a size or type that gives the needed baseline.
     107	- Instance level: some smaller instance sizes publish `EBSIOBalance%` and `EBSByteBalance%`. Draining or at 0 means the instance has dropped or will drop to its EBS baseline. Recommend an instance type whose baseline covers the measured demand.
     108	
     109	### How much IOPS or throughput to provision
     110	
     111	1. Measure peak demand per volume over a representative window (IOPS and MiB/s, Step 3 math).
     112	2. Apply the type rules (gp3: up to 500 IOPS per GiB and 0.25 MiB/s per IOPS; io2: up to 1,000 IOPS per GiB, and throughput up to 0.256 MiB/s per provisioned IOPS; io1: up to 50 IOPS per GiB) from [metrics-thresholds.md](metrics-thresholds.md). For io1 and io2, check that the IOPS value also gives the throughput limit the workload needs.
     113	3. Check the instance's remaining EBS baseline: baseline minus the measured usage of the other attached volumes.
     114	4. Propose the smaller of the measured need and what the instance can deliver. If the need exceeds the instance baseline, say so and recommend an instance type change.
     115	5. State how the target was computed.
     116	
     117	## Decision rules
     118	
     119	Use the binding-layer decision tree in [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md). The signatures are in [metrics-thresholds.md](metrics-thresholds.md).
     120	
     121	## What to report
     122	
     123	The verdict template in [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md). When the instance is the ceiling, the Answer says: "The volume has headroom; raising volume IOPS will not help; change the instance type." Never call a volume "saturated" when it is below its own limit.
     124	
     125	## Safety rules
     126	
     127	- This path is read-only. Any `ModifyVolume` or instance type change is a proposal with exact parameters, expected effect, cost direction and rollback. It runs only through a directed action approved on the approval card.
     128	- Never recommend more provisioning for an impairment or an injected-latency signature.
     129	- A typed "approve" in chat is not approval.
     130	
     131	## Sources
     132

     134	- Instance metrics: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/viewing_metrics_with_cloudwatch.html
     135	- Amazon EBS-optimized instances: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/ebs-optimized.html
     136	- Amazon EBS performance: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/ebs-performance.html
     137	- Volume initialization: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/ebs-initialize.html
     138	- Fast snapshot restore: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/ebs-fast-snapshot-restore.html
     139	- Volume status checks: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/monitoring-volume-status.html
     140	- AWS FIS actions: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/fis/latest/userguide/fis-actions-reference.html
     141	- Elastic Volumes: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/ebs-modify-volume.html and https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/01/amazon-ebs-up-to-four-volume-modifications/
     142	- gp3, gp2, io1 and io2 rules, including io1 and io2 throughput limits: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/general-purpose.html and https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/provisioned-iops.html

{"id": "d032c88dfefd4bf19539e6a3d608a8a8", "role": "user", "content": [{"text": "Fast agent report: a separate fast agent investigated this same incident in parallel and has finished. This is its whole final report, shared once. Nobody has checked it.

## Root cause
The binding dimension is throughput (MiB/s), not IOPS. Volume vol-0123456789abcdef0 is a 20 GiB gp3 volume set to the gp3 baseline of 3000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s. At about 16:15 UTC the batch job on i-1234567890abcdef0_3 (c6i.xlarge) started reading sequentially in 256 KiB chunks, with no writes. Reads went to about 131.1 MB/s, which is exactly 125 MiB/s, and stayed flat there for every 5-minute period. A ceiling that flat means the volume is capping the job. At that I/O size the job only needs about 500 IOPS, so the IOPS metrics look normal while the throughput limit throttles it. The read queue settled around 1.5 to 1.7 and each read took about 3 ms, which fits requests waiting on the throughput cap. The instance-level EBS limit is not involved: InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck is 0 and EBSByteBalance% is 99. The fix is to raise this volume's Throughput with ModifyVolume (an online change). Raising IOPS won't help. gp3 allows at most 0.25 MiB/s of throughput per provisioned IOPS, so with 3000 IOPS you can go up to 750 MiB/s; anything higher means raising IOPS too. The instance also caps the gain. A c6i.xlarge has a baseline EBS bandwidth of about 1,250 Mbps (about 156 MB/s), shared by all four attached volumes, and can burst to about 10 Gbps for a limited time. A long job can therefore only gain about 25% sustained over today's 125 MiB/s unless the instance also moves to a larger size or a type with more EBS bandwidth. Watch InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck and EBSByteBalance% after the change.
## Evidence
- EC2 DescribeVolumes: vol-0123456789abcdef0 is gp3, 20 GiB, Iops=3000, Throughput=125 MiB/s, attached to i-1234567890abcdef0_3 at /dev/sdg.
- Alarm example-b-gp3-read-bytes went to ALARM at 16:23:18Z. VolumeReadBytes Sum over 60 s was 7.87e9 bytes at 16:20, 16:21 and 16:22, which is about 131.1 MB/s = 125.0 MiB/s, the provisioned cap. The threshold is 6e9.
- AWS/EBS VolumeReadBytes (5-min Sum) was 0 from 15:30 to 16:10, rose to 4.18e9 at 16:15, then held at 39.34e9 per 5 min from 16:20 to 16:40 (about 125.07 MiB/s, varying by less than 0.01%).
- AWS/EBS VolumeReadOps (5-min Sum) was about 150,085 per 5 min, or about 500 IOPS, roughly 17% of the 3000 provisioned. Average I/O size is 39.34e9 / 150,086 = 262,144 B (256 KiB). VolumeWriteBytes and VolumeWriteOps were 0.
- AWS/EBS VolumeQueueLength was 0 before 16:15 and about 1.5 to 1.73 from 16:20 on. VolumeTotalReadTime / ReadOps works out to about 3.1 to 3.4 ms per read.
- AWS/EC2 InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck was 0 for the whole window and EBSByteBalance% stayed at 99, so the instance-level EBS limit is not the bottleneck.
## Affected resources
- vol-0123456789abcdef0
- i-1234567890abcdef0_3
- example-b-gp3-read-bytes
## Gaps
- VolumeThroughputExceededCheck and VolumeIOPSExceededCheck returned no datapoints, so the conclusion that throughput is the cap rests on the flat 125 MiB/s ceiling plus the queueing, not on a direct exceeded flag.
- I didn't verify the c6i.xlarge baseline and burst EBS bandwidth figures against current documentation. Confirm them before sizing the new throughput.
- I didn't examine the job's own logs, metrics or start trigger. The 16:15 start is inferred from the volume metrics.", "type": "text"}], "user_reference": null}

Indeed, EBSReadBytes on these Nitro instances is a 5-minute sum, so dividing by 60 instead of 300 inflates the value by exactly 5x — 132.9 × 5 = 664.5, which confirms the volume sum is correct.

Comparing against c6i.xlarge's baseline (~149 MiB/s, 6000 IOPS) and burst max (~1192 MiB/s, 40000 IOPS), the summed demand of 132.9 MiB/s sits at 89% of baseline with the EBSByteBalance% still at 99%, so the instance isn't the bottleneck. Instead, gp3 volume B appears pinned at its provisioned 125 MiB/s throughput while only using 17% of its IOPS allowance, pointing to the volume's throughput setting as the binding constraint — and I'm noting the io2 volume separately flatlined at its provisioned 1000 IOPS as another fixed ceiling.

For the io2 volume, the 1000 IOPS cap translates to a 256 MiB/s throughput limit, but it's only hitting 7.81 MiB/s — so it's IOPS-bound on small 8 KiB operations rather than throughput-bound, which is a distinct finding from volume B's situation.

I'm now checking whether raising gp3 volume B's throughput would actually help: since all EBS traffic shares the instance's baseline of ~149 MiB/s, and the other volumes already consume about 7.84 MiB/s of that, the realistic ceiling for volume B within baseline is only about 141 MiB/s — just a 13% gain, which barely seems worth recommending unless paired with an instance change. True demand for volume B is hard to pin down since it's already saturated at its cap; using queue depth (~1.5) and latency (~3ms at 256 KiB) as a rough proxy, actual demand if unthrottled could plausibly range anywhere from 250 to 750 MiB/s, which is too uncertain to state confidently.

I also note EBSByteBalance% sitting at 99 suggests burst capacity is available, letting the instance push up to ~1192 MiB/s temporarily, though the guidance is to size for sustained baseline, not burst. This leaves two paths: a safe but modest throughput bump to ~140 MiB/s on the current instance, or a more meaningful fix by upgrading to a larger instance type (c6i.2xlarge or c6i.4xlarge) with a much higher EBS baseline before raising the gp3 throughput further — I want to pull the actual baseline numbers for those instance types to confirm before recommending.

I should also pull the newer VolumeThroughputExceededCheck and InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck metrics directly with Maximum/60s granularity to get a clean confirmation signal, and double check that DescribeVolumesModifications showing no prior history for the other volume rules out recent config changes as a contributing factor. CloudTrail and AWS Health/FIS checks don't seem necessary here since this looks like a straightforward saturation pattern tied to the batch job's start time rather than an external impairment.

For cost, gp3 throughput above the 125 MiB/s baseline runs about $0.040 per MiB/s-month in us-east-1, so bumping to 140 or 250 MiB/s would only add a few dollars monthly — I'll give directional cost estimates rather than precise figures. Switching instance types like c6i.xlarge to c6i.2xlarge roughly doubles the on-demand hourly rate and requires a stop/start cycle, so I want to flag that downtime tradeoff. Let me pull describe_instance_types for the larger c6i options and query those exceeded-check metrics now.

{"id": "f363aff4-8d63-49ae-a1db-9e35fe06e152", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"thinking": "VolumeThroughputExceededCheck flips to 1 starting at 16:15, which is a clear signal of hitting the throughput cap, while IOPS-related checks stay at 0, ruling those out. Looking at instance metrics, throughput is at 132.9 MiB/s and 1,501 IOPS against a baseline of 149.0 MiB/s and 6,000 IOPS, with EBSByteBalance% sitting near 99, confirming the bottleneck is throughput rather than IOPS.

The root cause traces to the 125 MiB/s gp3 default throughput limit on volume B binding under a sequential 256 KiB read workload that kicked in around 16:18-16:19. For sizing a fix, I'm calculating headroom on the current c6i.xlarge baseline (149.01 MiB/s minus ~7.83 MiB/s used by other volumes leaves ~141.2 MiB/s, so bumping vol B to 140 MiB/s is the max this instance allows), and comparing against upgrading to c6i.2xlarge where the larger 298 MiB/s baseline would let me target something like 280 MiB/s throughput, which only needs about 1,120 IOPS at 256 KiB block size, well within gp3 limits.

Since the true workload demand is unknown while throughput is capped, I'm leaning toward a stepwise recommendation: upgrade to c6i.2xlarge with 280 MiB/s throughput, then monitor the VolumeThroughputExceededCheck metric, escalating to c6i.4xlarge if it's still saturated. I also want to flag burst throughput as a separate consideration — the current c6i.xlarge can burst to 1,192 MiB/s while EBSByteBalance% is still high, which could be a short-term alternative if the batch job is brief enough to finish before the burst balance drains back to baseline.

For implementation order, I'm noting that the instance type change requires a stop/start since it's EBS-backed, while ModifyVolume can be applied live. The plan would be to bump throughput to 140 MiB/s now within the current baseline, then schedule a maintenance window to resize to c6i.2xlarge and push throughput to 280 MiB/s — keeping in mind the 4-modifications-per-24h EBS limit, so two changes is comfortable, though going straight to 280 after the instance resize would save a modification. I'm also working out the cost delta: gp3 throughput above 125 MiB/s is billed per MiB/s-month, so 140 MiB/s adds about $0.60/month while 280 MiB/s adds roughly $6.20/month.

I'll flag that the instance upgrade roughly doubles the hourly compute cost, and since pricing isn't something I pulled from an API call, I should present it as directional and recommend verification rather than treating it as hard evidence. For rollback, I'd note reverting throughput back to 125 and reversing the instance type via stop/modify/start.

Separately, I'm noting the io2 volume is pinned at its provisioned 1,000 IOPS limit with steady 7.81 MiB/s throughput, which isn't the focus of the user's question but is already factored into the overall sizing — and CPU utilization at 1.2% confirms the job is I/O-bound rather than compute-bound.

EbsOptimized shows false in DescribeInstances, but since c6i is EBS-optimized by default, this has no real effect per AWS documentation — worth a brief mention. I'm also noting the alarm flapped earlier today and on a prior date, suggesting this is a recurring pattern tied to the same job run rather than a one-off.

On gaps: I haven't checked CloudTrail's ModifyVolume history, though DescribeVolumesModifications shows no modifications ever recorded for either volume, meaning they're still at their original creation settings.

Cross-checking the fast agent's claims against my own data, most hold up — throughput-bound, 256 KiB, 500 IOPS, ~1.5 queue depth, ~3ms latency, InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck at 0, EBSByteBalance at 99. But there are discrepancies: the fast agent claimed no data for VolumeThroughputExceededCheck when I actually found a value of 1, and it said reads started around 16:15 when my minute-level data shows reads beginning at 16:19. It also overstated the potential throughput gain — accounting for the io2 volume's baseline usage, the real headroom is closer to 13% rather than 25%.

I'm categorizing this as a Limits issue and now launching the mitigation subagent with these findings, in English, before wrapping up.

", "signature": "", "type": "thinking"}, {"text": "The volume's throughput limit is what's slowing the job, not IOPS. vol-0123456789abcdef0 is pinned at its 125 MiB/s gp3 throughput limit while using only about 17% of its 3,000 IOPS. Raising IOPS won't help. Raise the volume's throughput. But this c6i.xlarge's ongoing EBS bandwidth only leaves room for about 140 MiB/s, so a real speedup also needs a bigger instance.

**What the metrics show** (2026-11-23, UTC)
- **The volume:** gp3, 20 GiB, set to 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s, which are the gp3 defaults. It has never been modified.
- **When it started:** the volume was idle until 16:18. At 16:19 a sequential, read-only workload began. From 16:20 to 16:47 reads held flat at 125.04–125.10 MiB/s, exactly the limit.
- **Why IOPS looks normal:** each read is 256 KiB, so 125 MiB/s needs only about 500 IOPS.
- **Signs of a limit, not a fault:**
  - The volume was busy 100% of the time.
  - About 1.5 requests were waiting at any moment, and each read took about 3.0 ms.
  - The volume's status is ok and its stalled-I/O check is 0, so it isn't impaired.
- **Direct confirmation:** CloudWatch's "throughput exceeded" check for this volume reads 1 in every 5-minute period from 16:15 to 16:45. Its "IOPS exceeded" check reads 0.
- **The alarm itself:** 7.87e9 bytes per minute at 16:20, 16:21 and 16:22 equals 125.08 MiB/s. It went to ALARM at 16:23:18.

**The instance isn't the limit yet, but it caps how far you can go**
- **Current load:** all four attached volumes together read about 132.9 MiB/s and about 1,501 IOPS (16:20–16:45).
- **Instance allowance:** a c6i.xlarge's ongoing EBS allowance is 149.0 MiB/s (156.25 MB/s) and 6,000 IOPS. It can burst to 1,192 MiB/s for a limited time.
- **Instance health:** both EBS burst balances are at 99%, the instance-level "throughput exceeded" check is 0, and CPU is about 1.2%.

**What to change**
1. **Now, on the current instance:** raise the volume's throughput to 140 MiB/s and leave IOPS at 3,000. Room for this volume = 149.0 − 7.83 MiB/s used by the other volumes ≈ 141 MiB/s. That's only about a 12% gain. The change is online, costs a little more each month, and can be reverted to 125 once it completes.
2. **For a real speedup:** change the instance type to c6i.2xlarge (298.0 MiB/s and 12,000 IOPS ongoing), then set the volume's throughput to about 280 MiB/s.
   - That fits: 280 + 7.83 is under 298.
   - It's within the gp3 limit of 0.25 MiB/s per IOPS (up to 750 MiB/s at 3,000 IOPS).
   - At 256 KiB per read it needs only about 1,120 IOPS.
   - Changing the type needs a stop and start, so schedule it outside a job run. The instance will cost about twice as much per hour.
   - If the throughput-exceeded check still reads 1 afterwards, c6i.4xlarge allows up to 596.0 MiB/s.
3. Afterwards, check that the throughput-exceeded check drops to 0 and that the instance burst balances stay steady.

I've started a separate mitigation planner with these findings. It will deliver its plan separately, and any change runs only after you approve it.

**Other things I noticed**
- The io2 volume vol-1234567890abcdef0_4 is flat at its 1,000 IOPS limit (about 7.81 MiB/s). It shares the instance's EBS allowance and is counted in the sizing above.
- The same alarm fired earlier today (07:42–07:54 and 08:03–14:00) and on 2026-11-11. This looks like a recurring job that hits the same limit on every run.

**What I couldn't check**
- I didn't look up the volume's change history in CloudTrail. AWS only records the latest modification per volume, and it shows none for this one.
- The job's real throughput need is unknown because it has been capped the whole time. I didn't look at the job's own logs.
- I didn't look up current pricing, so the cost changes above are directions only.", "type": "text"}], "user_reference": null}

# Investigation Summary

## Symptoms

### Read-bytes alarm firing on gp3 volume vol-0123456789abcdef0
**Description:** The alarm example-b-gp3-read-bytes ([redacted ARN]) entered ALARM at 2026-11-23T16:23:18Z. The last 3 one-minute Sum datapoints (16:20–16:22) were 7.87e9, 7.868e9 and 7.87e9 bytes, all above the 6e9 threshold. The alarm has no actions.
**Time:** 2026-11-23T16:20:00Z

## Findings

### Root Cause: gp3 throughput limit (125 MiB/s) is capping the batch job
**Description:** vol-0123456789abcdef0 (gp3, 20 GiB, 3000 IOPS / 125 MiB/s defaults, never modified) is pinned at 125.04–125.10 MiB/s from 16:20–16:47 UTC while using only ~500 of 3000 IOPS (256 KiB sequential reads). VolumeThroughputExceededCheck = 1 every 5-min period from 16:15; VolumeIOPSExceededCheck = 0. Volume 100% busy, queue ~1.5, ~3.0 ms reads; status ok, stalled-I/O check 0. Raising IOPS won't help; the volume's Throughput must be raised. The c6i.xlarge EBS baseline (149.0 MiB/s) limits how far it can go.
**Cascades to:** symptom-gp3-read-bytes-alarm

#### Supporting Observations
- **Read throughput pinned at 125 MiB/s provisioned limit:** From 16:20 UTC, read throughput on vol-0123456789abcdef0 (VolumeReadBytes/60) holds at 125.04–125.10 MiB/s every minute, and VolumeAvgThroughput agrees at ~125.07 MiB/s. That equals the volume's provisioned gp3 throughput of 125 MiB/s. There are no writes. Before 16:19 the volume was idle.
- **IOPS at 500 of 3000; 256 KiB sequential reads, ~3 ms latency:** IOPS holds at ~500/s, which is 17% of the provisioned 3000. Read I/O size is a constant 256 KiB. # Mitigation Summary

## Action
Raise gp3 throughput on vol-0123456789abcdef0 from 125 to 140 MiB/s now (online, Iops stays 3000). In a window between batch runs, change i-1234567890abcdef0_3 from c6i.xlarge to c6i.2xlarge, then raise throughput to 280 MiB/s.

## Reasoning
Reads are flat at 125 MiB/s with VolumeThroughputExceededCheck = 1 while IOPS sits at ~500 of 3000, so raising IOPS would not help. The c6i.xlarge EBS baseline (149.0 MiB/s minus ~7.83 MiB/s used by other volumes) caps stage 1 at ~140 MiB/s (+12%). c6i.2xlarge doubles the baseline to 298.0 MiB/s, so 280 MiB/s fits and stays within gp3's 0.25 MiB/s-per-IOPS limit. The volume has 4 of 4 modifications available in the rolling 24h; stage 1, stage 2 and one rollback use 3.

## Execution Plan

### Step 1: Prepare

#### 1.1 Record the current volume config as the rollback baseline (expect gp3…
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-volumes --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --query 'Volumes[0].{Type:VolumeType,Size:Size,Iops:Iops,Throughput:Throughput,State:State,Attach:Attachments[0].InstanceId}'
```
**Purpose:** Record the current volume config as the rollback baseline (expect gp3, 20 GiB, 3000 IOPS, 125 MiB/s).

#### 1.2 Record the instance type and public IP before stage 2
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-instances --region us-east-1 --instance-ids i-1234567890abcdef0_3 --query 'Reservations[0].Instances[0].{Type:InstanceType,State:State.Name,PublicIp:PublicIpAddress}'
```
**Purpose:** Record the instance type and public IP before stage 2.
**Advisory:** Without an Elastic IP, the public IP changes after a stop/start.

#### 1.3 Confirm the volume still has modifications left (max 4 per rolling 24h)
**Type:** command
```
aws cloudtrail lookup-events --region us-east-1 --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=ResourceName,AttributeValue=vol-0123456789abcdef0 --start-time $(date -u -d '-24 hours' +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ) --query 'Events[?EventName==`ModifyVolume`].EventTime'
```
**Purpose:** Confirm the volume still has modifications left (max 4 per rolling 24h).

### Step 2: Pre Validate

#### 2.1 Ensure no modification is running; stop if state is 'modifying' or…
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0
```
**Purpose:** Ensure no modification is running; stop if state is 'modifying' or 'optimizing'.

### Step 3: Apply

#### 3.1 Stage 1: raise throughput to 140 MiB/s online, the most the c6i.xlarge…
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 modify-volume --region us-east-1 --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --throughput 140
```
**Purpose:** Stage 1: raise throughput to 140 MiB/s online, the most the c6i.xlarge baseline allows.
**Risks:** Only ~12% gain; job may remain throughput-bound. Small cost increase., Uses 1 of 4 modifications in the rolling 24h.
**Advisory:** New throughput applies during 'optimizing'; no need to wait for 'completed'.

#### 3.2 Stage 2: resize to c6i.2xlarge to double the EBS baseline to 298.0 MiB/s
**Type:** command
```
# Stage 2 — only in a window with no batch job running
aws ec2 stop-instances --region us-east-1 --instance-ids i-1234567890abcdef0_3
aws ec2 wait instance-stopped --region us-east-1 --instance-ids i-1234567890abcdef0_3
aws ec2 modify-instance-attribute --region us-east-1 --instance-id i-1234567890abcdef0_3 --instance-type '{"Value":"c6i.2xlarge"}'
aws ec2 start-instances --region us-east-1 --instance-ids i-1234567890abcdef0_3
aws ec2 wait instance-running --region us-east-1 --instance-ids i-1234567890abcdef0_3
```
**Purpose:** Stage 2: resize to c6i.2xlarge to double the EBS baseline to 298.0 MiB/s.
**Risks:** Downtime during stop/start; running jobs are interrupted., c6i.2xlarge costs ~2x on demand., On-Demand capacity in us-east-1a not guaranteed; if start fails, revert to c6i.xlarge.
**Advisory:** Ensure /dev/sdf, /dev/sdg, /dev/sdi mount by UUID or with nofail in /etc/fstab.

#### 3.3 Stage 2: raise throughput to 280 MiB/s once running as c6i.2xlarge
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 modify-volume --region us-east-1 --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --throughput 280
```
**Purpose:** Stage 2: raise throughput to 280 MiB/s once running as c6i.2xlarge.
**Risks:** Do not apply while still c6i.xlarge — the instance baseline becomes the bottleneck., Further cost increase; uses another modification.
**Advisory:** Real demand is unknown; size to the measured peak after the first run.

### Step 4: Post Validate

#### 4.1 Confirm the modification completes with Throughput 140 (280 after stage…
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --query 'VolumesModifications[0].{State:ModificationState,Progress:Progress,Target:TargetThroughput,Orig:OriginalThroughput}'
aws ec2 describe-volumes --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --query 'Volumes[0].{Iops:Iops,Throughput:Throughput}'
```
**Purpose:** Confirm the modification completes with Throughput 140 (280 after stage 2) and Iops 3000.

#### 4.2 After stage 2, confirm c6i.2xlarge is running with all 4 volumes…
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-instances --region us-east-1 --instance-ids i-1234567890abcdef0_3 --query 'Reservations[0].Instances[0].{Type:InstanceType,State:State.Name,Vols:BlockDeviceMappings[].Ebs.VolumeId}'
```
**Purpose:** After stage 2, confirm c6i.2xlarge is running with all 4 volumes attached.

#### 4.3 Confirm reads exceed 125 MiB/s and the instance throughput check stays 0
**Type:** command
```
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --region us-east-1 --namespace AWS/EBS --metric-name VolumeReadBytes --dimensions Name=VolumeId,Value=vol-0123456789abcdef0 --statistics Sum --period 60 --start-time $(date -u -d '-15 minutes' +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ) --end-time $(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --region us-east-1 --namespace AWS/EBS --metric-name VolumeThroughputExceededCheck --dimensions Name=VolumeId,Value=vol-0123456789abcdef0 Name=InstanceId,Value=i-1234567890abcdef0_3 --statistics Maximum --period 300 --start-time $(date -u -d '-30 minutes' +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ) --end-time $(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --region us-east-1 --namespace AWS/EC2 --metric-name InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck --dimensions Name=InstanceId,Value=i-1234567890abcdef0_3 --statistics Maximum --period 300 --start-time $(date -u -d '-30 minutes' +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ) --end-time $(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
```
**Purpose:** Confirm reads exceed 125 MiB/s and the instance throughput check stays 0.
**Advisory:** The read-bytes alarm (~95.4 MiB/s threshold) stays in ALARM after the fix; don't use it to judge success.

### Step 5: Rollback

#### 5.1 Restore the original 125 MiB/s throughput
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 modify-volume --region us-east-1 --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --throughput 125
```
**Purpose:** Restore the original 125 MiB/s throughput.
**Risks:** Brings back the original cap; counts toward the 4-per-24h limit.

#### 5.2 Restore the original c6i.xlarge instance type
**Type:** command
```
# Only if stage 2 was applied; lower the volume to ≤140 MiB/s first
aws ec2 stop-instances --region us-east-1 --instance-ids i-1234567890abcdef0_3
aws ec2 wait instance-stopped --region us-east-1 --instance-ids i-1234567890abcdef0_3
aws ec2 modify-instance-attribute --region us-east-1 --instance-id i-1234567890abcdef0_3 --instance-type '{"Value":"c6i.xlarge"}'
aws ec2 start-instances --region us-east-1 --instance-ids i-1234567890abcdef0_3
```
**Purpose:** Restore the original c6i.xlarge instance type.
**Risks:** Downtime during stop/start.

## Code Change Specification

### Requirements

#### 1. Make the higher gp3 throughput (and instance type, if stage 2 is applied) permanent in infrastructure-as-code
**Description:** vol-0123456789abcdef0 runs on the gp3 default of 125 MiB/s, which a recurring sequential read workload saturates. Set Throughput in the volume definition to the applied value (140, or 280 with c6i.2xlarge) and set the instance type to match, so a redeploy does not drift back.
**Acceptance Criteria:**
- IaC sets Throughput=140 (or 280) and Iops=3000 for the volume, and the instance type matches live state
- Planned volume throughput + other volumes' usage ≤ instance EBS baseline in MiB/s
- No drift between IaC and live state after deploy

#### 2. Rework the alarm so it flags the throughput cap, not ordinary job load
**Description:** example-b-gp3-read-bytes fires above ~95.4 MiB/s, below provisioned throughput. Replace it, or add alarms, on AWS/EBS VolumeThroughputExceededCheck (VolumeId+InstanceId) and AWS/EC2 InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck, or move the threshold close to provisioned throughput.
**Acceptance Criteria:**
- The alarm fires only when the volume or instance throughput limit is reached
- It does not fire during normal job runs under the provisioned limit

- Sizing math: remaining instance baseline for vol-0123456789abcdef0 on c6i.xlarge = 149.0 - 7.83 = about 141 MiB/s, so the largest throughput that stays within the current baseline is about 140 MiB/s (+12%). c6i.2xlarge baseline is 312.5 MB/s (298.0 MiB/s), 12,000 IOPS; c6i.4xlarge is 625 MB/s (596.0 MiB/s), 20,000 IOPS (both from DescribeInstanceTypes). On c6i.2xlarge, about 280 MiB/s for this volume fits within the baseline (280 + 7.83 < 298). gp3 rule: Throughput must not exceed 0.25 MiB/s per provisioned IOPS, so with 3000 IOPS the maximum is 750 MiB/s. 280 MiB/s at 256 KiB needs about 1,120 IOPS, which is within 3000.
- The job's unconstrained demand is unknown because it is pinned at the cap.
- The alarm also fired earlier today (07:42 to 07:54 and 08:03 to 14:00 UTC) and on 2026-11-11, so this workload recurs.

{"id": "bdefde45-2911-439d-a789-1a5fe43d8cc3", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_M6avoSeVZlXraKkh6zkNGg", "content": [{"text": "     1	---
     2	name: storage-ebs-expertise
     3	description: >
     4	  Use this skill when a user wants to know why Amazon EBS storage is slow, why an
     5	  EBS alarm fired, or whether their EBS setup is production-ready, even if they only
     6	  say an app or database on EC2 got slower or ask whether to add IOPS. Use it for
     7	  alarms on AWS/EBS metrics (VolumeReadOps, VolumeWriteOps, VolumeReadBytes,
     8	  VolumeWriteBytes, VolumeQueueLength, VolumeTotalReadTime/WriteTime,
     9	  VolumeAvgReadLatency, VolumeStalledIOCheck, BurstBalance) or
     10	  EBSIOBalance%/EBSByteBalance%; for sizing
     11	  IOPS or throughput changes; for requests to raise IOPS or modify a volume; for a
     12	  volume modification that looks stuck or failed; for deciding which snapshots or
     13	  AMIs need owner review before deletion, or how to recover them; for KMS errors
     14	  on encrypted volumes; for EBS quota or limit errors; for a jump in the EBS bill;
     15	  and for a pre-launch EBS review. Do not use it for S3, EFS, FSx, instance store,
     16	  or EC2 problems unrelated to EBS.
     17	metadata:
     18	  author: dewavic
     19	  version: "1.0.0"
     20	  summary: "Troubleshoot Amazon EBS performance, volume modifications, snapshots, encryption, quotas and cost, and review an account's EBS setup with read-only checks."
     21	  aws-devops-agent-skills.agent-types: "CHAT, INCIDENT_RCA"
     22	  aws-devops-agent-skills.aws-services: "Amazon EBS, Amazon EC2, Amazon CloudWatch, AWS CloudTrail, AWS Service Quotas"
     23	  aws-devops-agent-skills.technical-domains: "Storage"
     24	---
     25	# Amazon EBS Expertise
     26	
     27	Use this skill to troubleshoot Amazon EBS problems and to review an account's Amazon EBS setup. It has two modes. Troubleshoot mode answers "something is wrong, why?" through one of five paths and returns a fixed verdict. Review mode answers "is my EBS setup healthy before something goes wrong?" and returns a rated report. Both modes are read-only and share the same volume-type rules, instance limits and service rules. Load only the reference files the request needs.
     28	
     29	## When to Use This Skill
     30	
     31	- Storage-related slowness, timeouts or high I/O latency on an Amazon EC2 instance.
     32	- An alarm on AWS/EBS metrics or on instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%`.
     33	- A request to raise IOPS or throughput, or to modify a volume.
     34	- A volume modification that looks stuck, failed, or did not improve performance.
     35	- Snapshot, AMI, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, AWS Backup or Recycle Bin questions, including which snapshots need owner review before deletion.
     36	- Encrypted-volume access errors and AWS KMS questions for Amazon EBS.
     37	- Amazon EBS cost increases, idle or over-provisioned volumes.
     38	- An operation that failed on an Amazon EBS quota, or "how close am I to my limits?"
     39	- A request to review Amazon EBS posture before a launch, migration or peak event.
     40	
     41	Do not use this skill for Amazon S3, Amazon EFS, Amazon FSx, instance store, or Amazon EC2 issues unrelated to Amazon EBS.
     42	
     43	## Prerequisites
     44	
     45	- Read-only permissions for the APIs listed in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md).
     46	- AWS CloudTrail access is optional. The skill works without it.
     47	- Mutating changes run only through directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App), which need their own role and operator approval on the approval card.
     48	
     49	---
     50	
     51	## Workflow
     52	
     53	Copy this checklist and tick each step as you finish it:
     54	
     55	- [ ] Step 1: Classify the request
     56	- [ ] Step 2: Load the shared references
     57	- [ ] Step 3: Run the path and draft the report
     58	- [ ] Step 4: Check the draft, fix it, then present it
     59	
     60	## Step 1: Classify the Request
     61	
     62	| The user says or the alarm shows | Mode and path | Load |
     63	|---|---|---|
     64	| "My app is slow", high latency, an alarm on AWS/EBS metrics, `EBSIOBalance%` or `EBSByteBalance%`, "is it storage?", "how much IOPS do I need?" | Troubleshoot: performance | [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md) |
     65	| "My modification is stuck", "the new IOPS has not taken effect", a `ModifyVolume` error, resize, gp2 to gp3, extend the file system, shrink or cancel | Troubleshoot: volume modification | [references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md](references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md) |
     66	| "Which snapshots can I delete?", snapshot copy did not arrive, AMI creation stuck, recover a deleted snapshot or volume, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, Recycle Bin | Troubleshoot: snapshots | [references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md](references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md) |
     67	| "I can't attach my KMS-encrypted volume", share an encrypted snapshot or AMI, encryption by default, re-encrypt a volume | Troubleshoot: encryption | [references/troubleshoot-encryption.md](references/troubleshoot-encryption.md) |
     68	| "Why did my EBS bill go up?", unexplained charges, idle or unattached volumes, pricing model | Troubleshoot: billing | [references/troubleshoot-billing.md](references/troubleshoot-billing.md) |
     69	| "Limit exceeded", a quota error, "how close am I to my limits?" | Shared capability: quota headroom | [Capacity and quota headroom](references/review-operational.md#capacity-and-quota-headroom) |
     70	| "Are my volumes backed up?" | Review: resilience area | [Resilience](references/review-operational.md#resilience) |
     71	| "Review my EBS setup", "is my storage production-ready?" | Review | [references/review-operational.md](references/review-operational.md) and [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md) |
     72	
     73	If a request fits more than one row, answer the question the user asked first and treat the rest as Separate findings.
     74	
     75	## Step 2: Load the Shared References
     76	
     77	- Always load [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md) (read-only APIs, metric math, errors and fallbacks).
     78	- Load [references/metrics-thresholds.md](references/metrics-thresholds.md) for any metric judgement.
     79	- Load [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md) for the verdict, the binding layer, escalation and review ratings.
     80	- Load [references/ebs-best-practices.md](references/ebs-best-practices.md) for service rules (Elastic Volumes, instance limits, quotas, snapshots, quirks).
     81	
     82	## Step 3: Run the Path and Draft the Report
     83	
     84	Follow the numbered procedure in the loaded path. Discover every value from the APIs. Then draft the report in the format below.
     85	
     86	### Troubleshoot verdict format
     87	
     88	1. **Answer:** the asked question, answered first.
     89	2. **Evidence:** values with units and time window.
     90	3. **Binding layer:** Volume, Instance, Burst credits, Quota, Not EBS, AWS-side impairment (only with a direct signal, see [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md)), Indeterminate, or Not applicable.
     91	4. **Recommendation:** exact parameters, or "No change".
     92	5. **Separate findings:** other true facts that do not change the Answer.
     93	6. **Gaps:** what could not be checked and why.
     94	
     95	In an investigation, put the Answer and the Recommendation with its exact parameters in the root cause finding, not only under Gaps. Keep the findings on the resource the user asked about. Mention another volume only when it shares the same instance EBS baseline, and then as a Separate finding.
     96	
     97	When the Binding layer is Indeterminate, report it as one finding. Do not offer AWS-side impairment as a hypothesis. List each direct check you ran (volume status, `VolumeStalledIOCheck`, AWS Health, AWS FIS) with its result as supporting evidence, say that no check confirms or rules out an EBS-side slowdown, and give the escalation path.
     98	
     99	Review mode uses the rated report in [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md). Every Review mode response MUST begin with its Summary table, which rates all six areas (capacity and quota headroom, observability, cost hygiene, resilience, encryption posture, deletion protection), even when an area has no findings or is `Indeterminate`. The Summary table is required, not optional. Do not open with prose or an offer to run the review; start with the table, then the per-area detail.
     100	
     101	## Step 4: Check the Draft Before Presenting It
     102	
     103	Review the draft from Step 3 against these checks. Fix anything that fails, then present it.
     104	
     105	- Every number under Evidence came from an API call made in this session, has its unit and time window, and matches the resource ID it is attributed to.
     106	- The Binding layer agrees with the Evidence: the named layer is the one at its limit, and the other layers were checked and shown to have headroom. The Evidence gives the instance EBS baseline in MiB/s and IOPS next to the summed demand of all attached volumes.
     107	- Any Recommendation stays within the instance's EBS baseline and the volume type's documented limits, and it is not more provisioning for an impairment.
     108	- Every snapshot tier is backed by the checks it requires; if one of those checks failed, the item is not listed for owner review. No snapshot is recommended for deletion; the owner confirms first.
     109	- A review answer starts with the Summary table and rates all six areas.
     110	- Every API that failed or was not called is listed under Gaps.
     111	
     112	---
     113	
     114	## Critical Rules
     115	
     116	- **Read-only.** Changes (ModifyVolume, quota requests) are proposed with exact parameters, cost and rollback, and run only through operator-approved directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App). Approval is given only on the approval card. A typed "approve" in chat is not approval.
     117	- **Deletes are manual customer steps.** AWS DevOps Agent refuses delete-class operations (for example DeleteSnapshot, DeleteVolume, DeregisterImage), so never propose them as directed actions. After the owner confirms they no longer need the resource, give the commands for the customer to run with their own credentials.
     118	- **Answer in one reply.** In chat, run the checks in this conversation and return the finished verdict or report as your reply. Do not hand the work to a background sub-agent and reply with a "started" or "I will report back" message, because that message becomes the answer the user sees first.
     119	- **Discover, don't assume:** read every configuration value from the APIs.
     120	- **Rule EBS in or out before tuning it.**
     121	- **Answer the asked question first;** other findings go under "Separate findings".
     122	- **Review mode starts with the Summary table.** Every Review mode response begins with the Summary table of all six rated areas. The table is required, not optional.
     123	- **Always check the instance layer** and size changes within the instance's EBS **baseline**.
     124	- **Never recommend more provisioning for an impairment.**
     125	- **Use current service rules:** up to 4 Elastic Volumes modifications per volume per rolling 24 hours. There is no fixed waiting period between modifications; the next one is allowed once the previous one completes.
     126	- **No interpretation without data:** report what couldn't be checked and use fallbacks. `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the most recent modification per volume; modification history and counts come from the optional AWS CloudTrail `ModifyVolume` events, or are listed under Gaps.
     127	- **Units:** MiB/s for throughput, stated every time.
     128	- **Escalate** on scope signals or when the investigation can't explain the symptom.
     129	
     130	## Gotchas
     131	
     132	- A modification in `optimizing` is not stuck. The new size, IOPS or throughput already applies while it optimizes.
     133	- `DescribeInstanceTypes` reports EBS bandwidth in MB/s. Convert it to MiB/s before comparing it with volume throughput.
     134	- On io1 and io2, `VolumeThroughputPercentage` is the percentage of provisioned IOPS delivered. It is not a throughput signal.
     135	- `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `VolumeAvgReadLatency` and `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` need both `VolumeId` and `InstanceId` and exist only on Nitro instances. `VolumeAvgThroughput` is in KiB/s. `VolumeTotalReadTime` and `VolumeTotalWriteTime` are in seconds.
     136	- Rising latency and queue length with falling IOPS is not proof of an AWS-side impairment. Without a direct signal (failed `VolumeStalledIOCheck`, impaired volume status, or an open AWS Health event) and without a running AWS FIS experiment, the Binding layer is Indeterminate.
     137	- `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the latest modification per volume. It cannot count modifications in the last 24 hours.
     138	- `ListRecoveryPointsByResource` without `ManagedByAWSBackupOnly` set to true also lists snapshots that AWS Backup did not create.
     139	- A snapshot whose source volume is gone may be the only remaining copy of the data. List it for owner review; never call it safe to delete.
     140	- Snapshots are incremental, so deleting one may free less storage than its size suggests.
     141	
     142	## Error Handling
     143	
     144	Errors, gated reads and missing metrics are handled with the fallback table in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md). Name every failed API under Gaps and continue with the rest.
     145	
     146	## References
     147	
     148	- [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md): performance attribution, the live-tested procedure
     149	- [references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md](references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md): snapshot tiers (owner review), copy, AMI, lifecycle and recovery
     150	- [references/troubleshoot-encryption.md](references/troubleshoot-encryption.md): AWS KMS access, sharing encrypted snapshots, default encryption
     151	- [references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md](references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md): modification states, limits, errors, sizing, file system extension
     152	- [references/troubleshoot-billing.md](references/troubleshoot-billing.md): cost breakdown, change records, right-sizing
     153	- [references/review-operational.md](references/review-operational.md): Review mode checks and the quota headroom capability
     154	- [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md): read-only API allowlist, metric math, errors, fallbacks
     155	- [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md): verdict template, binding layer, escalation, review ratings
     156	- [references/metrics-thresholds.md](references/metrics-thresholds.md): documented limits and how to judge each volume type
     157	- [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md): rated report layout for Review mode
     158	- [references/ebs-best-practices.md](references/ebs-best-practices.md): volume-type rules, quotas, Elastic Volumes rules, quirks"}], "status": "success", "type": "tool_result"}, {"id": "tooluse_eEIgJM5IcLLlpGHnG4RCNm", "content": [{"text": "Successfully loaded /aidevops/skills/system/proposing-mitigations/references/evaluating-plans.md"}], "status": "success", "type": "tool_result"}], "user_reference": null}
